vignette: The sky turns the color of bruised iron, and Samuel's breath catches before the first drop falls. He is sixty-five now, standing in the produce aisle of his neighborhood retail store, straightening heads of lettuce. But thirty-one years ago, the sky had turned that exact shade, and the world had dissolved into water. He remembers the roar first, a wall of brown floodwater tearing through the coastal village where his grandparents had built a life, swallowing the ground floor of his home and the small hardware shop where he had worked for nine years. He remembers wading through chest-deep current, gripping the rusted railing of his second-story balcony as the water receded to reveal splintered furniture and his younger brother's face, pale and still in the mud. He had survived. The shop had not. The house had not. The silence that followed was heavier than the water. For decades, Samuel built a careful architecture of avoidance. He moved inland, took a different job, and anchored himself to the predictable rhythms of retail work. He prefers the morning shift, when the automatic doors whisper and the store is quiet enough to hear his own breathing. The work demands nothing but repetition: scanning barcodes, aligning price tags, wiping down checkout belts. He tells himself this predictability is safety. But the weather has never stopped speaking to him. When the evening news shows radar maps blooming with green and yellow, his shoulders hike toward his ears. He catches himself pacing the back storage room, counting the exits, checking the drainage grates along the loading dock. His wife, Adesuwa, says he flinches when she turns on the kitchen tap. He does not remember choosing to become this way. He only knows that water, wind, and the smell of wet asphalt pull him backward into a room where the air is thick and impossible to breathe. At sixty-five, his knees protest the fluorescent-lit aisles, and the store's overhead hum grates against his temples. He counts inventory with methodical precision, trying to outrun the images that slip through during lulls: a customer dropping a rain-slicked umbrella, a spill near the entrance, the sudden crack of thunder rolling across the sky. His hands remember the weight of wet lumber, the slick grip of submerged crates. His mind replays the aftermath, frame by frame, even when his feet move automatically toward the next cart. He tells himself it is just part of growing older, part of working retail, part of being a man who has carried too many years in his chest. He does not say that the memories arrive without warning, that his pulse quickens when the wind shifts, that he has stopped buying raincoats or checking sky apps because he needs to know what the clouds are bringing before they arrive. The store becomes a map he navigates by habit, every corner familiar, every sound monitored. He laughs at a coworker's joke sometimes, but the sound feels detached, like it belongs to someone else standing just outside the door. His uniform shirt sticks to his back by mid-afternoon, and he finds himself checking the ceiling tiles for water stains, a habit that hasn't faded with age. At home, Adesuwa knows to leave the bedroom window cracked even in winter. She knows to speak softly when the forecast calls for heavy rain, and she knows not to reach for him in his sleep. They have shared thirty-six years, but the space between them has grown quiet. He watches her turn in her sleep and feels a hollow ache, a longing to close the distance that his body refuses to bridge. Instead, he lies on his side, listening to the house settle, counting the drips from the gutter, rehearsing the inventory list until his mind goes flat. He wakes before dawn, pours two cups of coffee, and checks the weather app three times before the alarm sounds. The store opens in four hours. The registers will chime. The carts will roll. He will stand behind the counter and wait for the sky to stop speaking, knowing it never truly does, only changes its voice.
